paragraphs: This paper explains v-SVM classification through the geometry of the training data. A convex hull is the region formed by taking convex combinations of a set of points. The authors introduce subsets of these regions called soft convex hulls, whose extent is controlled by the parameter v. Training can then be understood as seeking maximal separation between these subsets.

The interpretation distinguishes two cases. When the original convex hulls do not intersect, the separating hyperplane lies halfway between them and maximizes their separation measured along its normal direction. When the hulls overlap, the soft convex hulls still determine the normal direction, while the hyperplane's offset is adjusted to minimize the error sum. This separates the questions of orientation and placement.

The geometric account also yields necessary and sufficient conditions for some choice of v to produce a nontrivial solution. Its contribution is therefore both explanatory and theoretical: it gives the parameter a geometric meaning and characterizes when a nontrivial classifier can exist.
neurips-1999-a-geometric-interpretation-.tldr: The paper interprets v-SVM through soft convex hulls and characterizes when a parameter choice yields a nontrivial classifier.

paragraphs: Bayesian model selection and averaging require reasoning about uncertainty in models, rather than committing immediately to one fitted configuration. This paper presents a practical framework for probabilistic graphical models that approximates posterior distributions over parameters, model structures, and latent variables. It therefore addresses several sources of uncertainty within a single analytical approach.

The posterior approximations emerge from a free-form optimization procedure that naturally accommodates conjugate priors. They are generally non-Gaussian, unlike the large-sample approximations discussed in the abstract, and the method does not require computing a Hessian. Predictive quantities can also be obtained analytically, connecting the approximated uncertainty directly to predictions.

The resulting algorithm extends Expectation Maximization and has a convergence guarantee. That guarantee concerns convergence of the algorithm; the framework still approximates the full Bayesian posterior. Applications include mixture models and source separation across several domains. The central contribution is a common computational framework that makes Bayesian selection, averaging, and prediction accessible across a broad class of graphical models.
neurips-1999-a-variational-baysian-frame.tldr: A variational framework analytically approximates Bayesian uncertainty over graphical-model parameters, structures, and latent variables.

paragraphs: Hierarchical learning machines can be non-identifiable: different parameter choices can describe the same underlying statistical model. The paper studies this setting through the geometry of the parameter sets representing the truth. These sets contain singularities, so their structure is more complicated than a smooth, regular parameter space.

Using algebraic analysis, the author proves an asymptotic expression for stochastic complexity. Its dependence on training sample size includes a leading logarithmic term and a correction involving the logarithm of the logarithm. The coefficients are a rational number and an integer tied to the singular structure. Thus, the analysis describes complexity through more than simply the number of adjustable parameters.

The paper also shows that these coefficients can be calculated algorithmically using resolution of singularities, a technique from algebraic geometry. It bounds the positive leading coefficient by half the parameter count and places the integer between one and that count. These are asymptotic theoretical results, providing a way to analyze the statistical complexity of non-regular learning machines.
neurips-1999-algebraic-analysis-for-non-.tldr: Algebraic geometry yields an asymptotic characterization of stochastic complexity for non-identifiable learning machines.

paragraphs: This paper presents an electronic system for detecting the periodicity of sound: the time interval over which a sound pattern repeats. Its design combines three types of analog VLSI building blocks: a silicon cochlea, two inner-hair-cell circuits, and two spiking neuron chips. These components form a hardware approach to extracting temporal structure from an acoustic input.

The silicon cochlea contains a cascade of filters. Two of its outputs have a relative delay, and spike trains generated from those outputs become synchronized only over a narrow range of sound periodicities. Selectivity therefore comes from the relationship between timing in the two output pathways. The system uses that synchrony to identify particular repetition intervals.

The stated advantage concerns the relationship between selectivity and response speed. Traditional band-pass filters trade greater selectivity against slower response, whereas the proposed system is described as responding quickly independently of selectivity. The contribution is a periodicity-extraction mechanism in which a narrow timing preference does not impose that conventional response-time tradeoff.
neurips-1999-an-analog-vlsi-model-of-per.tldr: An analog auditory circuit extracts sound periodicity through spike synchrony while maintaining fast responses independently of selectivity.

paragraphs: Training a regression support vector machine involves solving an optimization problem. This paper develops a decomposition algorithm that approaches training through smaller working sets. Building on existing decomposition principles, it focuses on how to choose those sets effectively, making working-set selection the central algorithmic question.

The authors derive new criteria for testing the optimality of a working set. From these criteria, they propose a selection principle called maximal inconsistency, intended to construct approximately optimal sets. The theoretical criteria therefore guide which part of the training problem the algorithm should address, rather than leaving this choice disconnected from optimality.

Experiments show superior performance relative to traditional regression SVM training without decomposition. The abstract also notes that similar findings had previously been reported for decomposition in pattern-recognition SVMs. The proposed method extends to regression-based SVM formulations for density estimation and integral equations. Its contribution combines a principled selection rule with empirical evidence for decomposition in regression training, without establishing superiority over every alternative decomposition method.
neurips-1999-an-improved-decomposition-a.tldr: A maximal-inconsistency rule selects approximately optimal working sets for decomposition-based regression SVM training.

paragraphs: The authors built and successfully tested a system that emulates aspects of a moving eye. An optical device shifts an image sensor's field of view by as much as 45 degrees in any direction. Four neuromorphic analog VLSI circuits, together with off-the-shelf electronics, implement the control loop that directs this movement.

The custom circuits communicate mainly through non-arbitrated address-event buses. The integrated system supports two distinct behaviors: rapid exploration directed by visual saliency and smooth pursuit of light spots. These behaviors demonstrate both shifts toward visually prominent locations and continued tracking of a moving target within one hardware system.

Reported saccades last between 45 and 100 milliseconds, a range described as comparable to human eye performance. Smooth pursuit works for light sources moving at up to 50 degrees per second in the visual field. These findings establish concrete operating capabilities for the tested device. The comparison with human performance concerns saccade duration, while the pursuit result specifically concerns moving light sources.
neurips-1999-an-oculo-motor-system-with-.tldr: A tested multi-chip analog system performs saliency-driven eye-like movements and smooth tracking of moving light sources.

paragraphs: This paper develops a class of approximate inference algorithms for two-layer graphical models of the QMR-DT type. Inference is the task of drawing probabilistic conclusions within a model. The contribution addresses how this computation can be approximated for the network family under study, with particular attention to understanding algorithmic convergence.

The authors give convergence rates for their algorithms and for the existing Jaakkola and Jordan algorithm. A rate describes how convergence proceeds, adding information beyond whether an algorithm converges at all. They also test the theoretical predictions empirically, linking the mathematical analysis to observed computational behavior.

Experiments on the difficult QMR-DT network problem find that the new algorithms perform roughly comparably to the Jaakkola and Jordan method. The stated result supports them as alternatives with analyzed convergence behavior, rather than as a demonstrated performance breakthrough over that method. The paper's value lies in combining a new algorithm family, rate analysis covering both new and existing approaches, and empirical checks on a challenging inference problem.
neurips-1999-approximate-inference-a-lgo.tldr: New approximate inference algorithms for QMR-DT-type networks have analyzed convergence rates and empirically comparable performance to an existing method.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a way to give the hidden states of a hidden Markov model an explicit neighborhood structure. Each state corresponds to a region in an imagined topology space. States are neighbors when their regions are connected, giving the model a geometric notion of which states can follow one another.

The transition matrix is constrained so that movement is allowed only between neighboring states. Consequently, every valid sequence of hidden states traces a connected path through the topology space. This turns an abstract spatial relationship into a concrete restriction on temporal behavior: the hidden sequence must respect the connections built into the model.

The author shows how these constrained models can discover underlying structure in complex sequences of high-dimensional observations. The application is recovering mouth movements from the acoustics of continuous speech. Here, the model connects a sequence of observed sounds with hidden movement structure. The central idea is to make connectivity part of sequence modeling, so that learning operates over paths with an organized topology.
neurips-1999-constrained-hidden-markov-m.tldr: Constraining hidden Markov transitions to neighboring states creates connected latent paths that can reveal structure in complex sequences.

paragraphs: This paper proposes methods for visualizing high-dimensional non-Gaussian data and selecting useful input variables. The methods draw on joint mutual information and independent component analysis. They address two related tasks: finding informative two-dimensional views of a dataset and choosing variables to supply to a classifier.

For visualization, the proposed algorithms can find multiple useful two-dimensional projections that existing methods do not easily identify. This matters because interpreting high-dimensional data can depend on which viewing coordinates are chosen. For variable selection, the reported advantage is better removal of input redundancy than methods based on simple mutual information. Joint information makes relationships among inputs relevant to the selection process.

The authors illustrate the methods on a radar signal analysis problem. They use the techniques both to choose viewing coordinates and to select inputs for a neural network classifier. The stated evidence supports the usefulness of the methods for those tasks in that application. The feature-selection claim specifically concerns eliminating redundancy, rather than a quantified improvement in classifier accuracy.
neurips-1999-data-visualization-and-feat.tldr: Joint mutual information and ICA support informative two-dimensional views and less redundant feature selection for non-Gaussian data.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether methods for inferring small gene-regulation networks can be adapted to large microarray datasets. Its evidence is preliminary. The approach first groups genes with similar expression trajectories into a minimal set of coexpressed clusters, shifting the modeling task from individual genes to the average behavior of gene groups.

A continuous-time analog recurrent neural network represents the clusters' mean expression trajectories under the different measurement conditions. The regulatory model is fitted using simulated annealing with weight decay. The procedure then examines several fitted models for common features in their connection matrices, making shared structure across fits part of the analysis.

The intended use includes assessing whether gene-expression time-course datasets are adequate for determining regulatory relationships such as coregulation. This connects the inference problem to the information available in the measurements themselves. The contribution is a proposed route from large collections of expression trajectories to candidate relationships among gene classes, supported by preliminary evidence that the adaptation from smaller-scale methods is feasible.
neurips-1999-from-coexpression-to-coregu.tldr: A preliminary workflow clusters gene-expression trajectories and compares fitted recurrent models to investigate regulation among gene classes.

paragraphs: Unsupervised model selection can involve deciding both which features matter and how many clusters the data contain. This paper presents a Bayesian approach that determines these two elements together. Treating them jointly makes the representation of the data part of model selection, alongside the choice of clustering structure.

The Bayesian scheme uses marginal likelihood as its objective. The authors derive a closed-form expression by assuming suitable forms for the likelihood and prior. This analytical result is conditional on those modeling choices. They compare the scheme with an alternative based on cross-validated likelihood, giving two different ways to evaluate candidate unsupervised models.

Extensive experiments compare the approaches, and the results are checked against ground truth. In those experiments, the Bayesian scheme using the proposed objective performs better than cross-validation. The finding supports that particular scheme in the tested settings; it does not establish that every Bayesian selection method will outperform cross-validation. The main contribution is a tractable joint selection approach backed by direct empirical comparisons.
neurips-1999-generalized-model-selection.tldr: A Bayesian objective jointly selects features and cluster count, outperforming cross-validated likelihood in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo estimation uses samples to approximate quantities associated with a probability distribution. This paper proposes a simple variation of importance sampling that explicitly searches for important regions of the target distribution. Its central idea is to concentrate sampling effort where samples contribute more significantly to the estimation task.

Searching for important regions changes how samples are allocated, making the correctness of the resulting estimate a central question. The author proves that the technique yields unbiased estimates. Unbiasedness means that the estimator's average over repeated sampling agrees with the quantity being estimated; it does not mean that each individual estimate is exact.

The paper also gives empirical evidence that this concentration of samples can reduce the variance of standard Monte Carlo estimators. Lower variance means less fluctuation between repeated estimates. The evidence therefore combines a proven property with an observed benefit: unbiasedness is established theoretically, while variance reduction is demonstrated empirically as something the method can achieve. The contribution connects active search for significant regions with valid Monte Carlo estimation.
neurips-1999-greedy-importance-sampling-.tldr: Greedy importance sampling searches significant regions while preserving unbiasedness and can empirically reduce estimator variance.

paragraphs: Comparisons between learning algorithms often use significance tests to judge whether observed performance differences are meaningful. This paper identifies a source of variability that many such tests neglect: changing the training set can change the learned model and its performance. Uncertainty in evaluation therefore includes uncertainty arising from which examples were used for learning.

The authors theoretically investigate the variance of the cross-validation estimate of generalization error while accounting for training-set variability. Generalization error concerns performance beyond the training data, and cross-validation provides an estimate of it. Analyzing the variance asks how much that estimate itself can fluctuate under the relevant sources of randomness.

The analysis leads to two proposed variance estimators. Simulations show that these statistics perform well relative to the statistics considered by Dietterich. The contribution is thus both an account of an overlooked source of uncertainty and practical ways to estimate its effect. The empirical finding concerns the proposed statistics in simulations, supporting more informed uncertainty assessment when comparing learning algorithms.
neurips-1999-inference-for-the-generaliz.tldr: Two variance estimators account for training-set variability when assessing cross-validation estimates of generalization error.

paragraphs: The paper treats image retrieval as Bayesian inference: a system uses available evidence to reason about which images match a user's interests. This formulation brings two difficult design problems into one framework. A user may care about a region within an image, and their judgments during a search session can clarify what they want.

For region-based queries, the approach does not require images to have been segmented beforehand. This matters because supporting a query about part of an image need not depend on a prior division of the entire image into regions. The Bayesian formulation is presented as providing a natural and effective solution to this retrieval requirement.

The authors also introduce a learning algorithm based on belief propagation to incorporate feedback. It accounts for both examples the user likes and examples the user rejects, allowing both kinds of evidence to inform the session. The contribution is a probabilistic treatment that connects region-level search with learning from user responses, rather than treating feedback as separate from the retrieval problem.
neurips-1999-learning-from-user-feedback.tldr: A Bayesian image-retrieval framework supports region queries without prior segmentation and learns from positive and negative user feedback.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to summarize a process's past while retaining information useful for predicting its future. Its information-theoretic approach learns a compact statistic from past states. That statistic serves as a condensed representation for modeling and distinguishing dynamic processes, making predictive information central to what the representation preserves.

Prediction uncertainty is described nonparametrically through a joint density over the learned statistic and the present observation. The method therefore learns both a useful summary and a probabilistic description relating that summary to observations. The authors consider noise-driven dynamical systems as well as random processes whose sampling distributions depend on their histories.

For the first setting, reported results capture both random-walk dynamics and the statistics of the driving noise. For the second, the method learns summaries of noisy random telegraph waves with different dependencies on past states. Together, these examples support a principled way to distinguish processes through their dynamics or historical dependencies. The contribution links compact predictive representations with an explicit account of uncertainty.
neurips-1999-learning-informative-statis.tldr: An information-theoretic method learns compact predictive summaries and nonparametric uncertainty descriptions for dynamic processes.

paragraphs: This paper explores the computational role of long-term depression, or LTD, in learning. Long-term potentiation, or LTP, strengthens synaptic connections and has long been associated with associative learning. LTD concerns weakening those connections. The study asks how time-dependent strengthening and weakening interact when considered together in small networks.

The motivation includes evidence that LTD occurs when a presynaptic cell fires after the postsynaptic cell. This makes the relative timing of neural activity important to the direction of synaptic change. Earlier laboratories had proposed modification kernels for LTP and LTD based on studies involving one postsynaptic unit. Such kernels describe how timing relates to the modification of a connection.

The paper moves the investigation to interactions within small networks, where both forms of plasticity operate together. Its title frames LTD as facilitating learning in a noisy environment, while the abstract specifies the computational question and network setting. The substantive focus is how weakening participates alongside strengthening in learning, with temporal order organizing the interaction between the two.
neurips-1999-ltd-facilitates-learning-in.tldr: The paper studies how timing-dependent synaptic strengthening and weakening interact in small networks, exploring LTD's role in learning.

paragraphs: Clustering is useful when the structure extracted from one sample reflects the source that generated the data. This paper frames reliability in terms of reproducibility: another sample from the same source should reveal similar structure. It investigates overfitting in maximum-entropy annealing algorithms using a class of histogram clustering models.

The analysis uses Bernstein's inequality, a bound on large deviations, to determine the maximally achievable approximation quality. That quality is parameterized through a minimum temperature. Temperature therefore becomes a way to express the limit on how finely the model should adapt while maintaining the statistical reliability sought by the analysis.

The resulting model-selection criterion uses annealing at a finite temperature. Monte Carlo simulations support the proposed criterion, connecting the theoretical argument to observed behavior in the studied setting. The contribution is a statistical basis for controlling clustering detail: extracted structure should remain representative of the data source. Its conclusions arise from the specified histogram models and annealing framework, rather than from an unrestricted claim about all clustering algorithms.
neurips-1999-model-selection-in-clusteri.tldr: A concentration-bound analysis motivates finite-temperature annealing to control overfitting in histogram clustering.

paragraphs: The paper applies stochastic meta-descent to independent component analysis for separating mixtures that change over time. The underlying challenge is that different sources can change their mixture coefficients at very different speeds. A learning procedure needs to adjust to these differences even when the rates of change are not known beforehand.

Stochastic meta-descent adapts local learning rates online and is presented for arbitrary twice-differentiable systems. It uses full second-order information while retaining linear computational complexity through efficient Hessian-vector products. This gives the adaptation access to curvature information without requiring the computational cost of explicitly manipulating a full Hessian matrix.

In the source-separation application, individual learning rates are matched to how quickly each source's mixture coefficients change. The resulting technique can simultaneously track sources moving at substantially different, initially unknown speeds. The important connection is between local adaptation and uneven change in the signal mixture: different parts of the learning process can respond on different time scales instead of sharing one fixed rate.
neurips-1999-online-independent-componen.tldr: Locally adapted learning rates let online ICA track time-varying mixtures whose sources change at different unknown speeds.

paragraphs: This paper proposes that recurrent competition in primary visual cortex changes during the response to a stimulus. Fast synaptic depression weakens recurrent excitation after stimulus onset. In the proposed account, this moves the network from an initially strongly nonlinear operating regime toward a more linear one.

The two phases serve different processing roles. Strong early competition establishes sharp orientation tuning and extracts salient stimulus features. Later, weaker competition permits precise signaling of multiple orientations and modulation through longer-range connections, including surround effects. The network therefore begins with prominent features and subsequently processes more detail, rather than maintaining the same competitive strength throughout its response.

The authors show that this processing strategy is optimal under a specified information-transmission objective and constraint. Neurons must have limited bandwidth, and the objective is to maximize information transmitted over any time interval beginning at stimulus onset. This conditional result gives the proposed temporal sequence a computational rationale. It does not make weakening competition universally optimal; the conclusion depends on the stated bandwidth restriction and objective.
neurips-1999-recurrent-cortical-competit.tldr: A proposed decline in cortical competition supports early feature selection followed by detail processing, with conditional information-theoretic optimality.

paragraphs: A model of a chaotic time series can predict the next few observations well yet reproduce the wrong attractor. The attractor describes the structure within which the system's dynamics evolve. This paper addresses the gap between minimizing short-term prediction errors and reproducing that larger dynamical structure.

The proposed approach learns short-term prediction and the outlines of the attractor simultaneously. It identifies those outlines using a new form of nonlinear principal component analysis. Closed-loop predictions are constrained to remain within the learned outlines, with the aim of preventing the predicted dynamics from diverging away from the attractor.

The authors report fast parameter estimation on a 1,000-sample laser dataset from the Santa Fe time-series competition: less than one minute on a 166 MHz Pentium PC. This is a concrete timing result for that example. The broader methodological contribution is to incorporate attractor structure directly into learning and prediction, addressing a property that short-term prediction accuracy alone does not guarantee.
neurips-1999-robust-learning-of-chaotic-.tldr: Jointly learning short-term predictions and attractor outlines constrains closed-loop chaotic forecasts to remain within the learned dynamical region.

paragraphs: People can generalize a concept by abstracting a rule or by comparing a new case with remembered examples. This paper argues that these apparently different approaches can both be understood as special cases of Bayesian learning. The proposed unification concerns the reasoning underlying generalization, rather than merely grouping two strategies under a shared label.

The Bayesian account addresses which rules are extracted and how similarity to examples is measured. It also explains why different situations should produce behavior that appears more rule-based or more similarity-based. Under this view, the form of generalization depends on the situation within a broader probabilistic framework.

The analysis nevertheless leaves a role for distinguishing rules from similarity at the algorithmic level. The distinction may be useful when constructing principled approximations to fully Bayesian learning, even if it is not fundamental to the underlying computation. The contribution is therefore a conceptual account that unifies the two modes while explaining why separate practical procedures for them may still be valuable.
neurips-1999-rules-and-similarity-in-con.tldr: Rule-based and similarity-based concept learning are presented as special cases of a common Bayesian framework.

paragraphs: This paper extends theoretical work on learning with linear functions, including settings connected to neural networks and support vector machines. Its central result is a set of dimension-independent covering-number bounds for regularized linear functions. A covering number measures how many representative functions are needed to approximate a function class at a chosen resolution.

The bounds hold under particular regularization conditions. Their significance is that the stated complexity control does not depend on dimension, provided those conditions apply. The authors show that the bounds lead to a class of methods for training linear classifiers with theoretical advantages similar to those of support vector machines.

The paper also analyzes these methods from an asymptotic statistical perspective, examining their behavior as sample sizes become large. This complements the covering-number approach with a description of large-sample behavior. The contribution links conditional complexity bounds to new training methods and then studies those methods through a second theoretical lens; the abstract's comparison with support vector machines concerns theoretical advantages.
neurips-1999-some-theoretical-results-co.tldr: Conditional dimension-independent complexity bounds motivate new regularized linear classifiers and an analysis of their large-sample behavior.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify a simple region containing most of the probability mass of a data distribution. The target is set by a chosen probability that a new observation falls outside this region. Because the training data are unlabelled, the task is to estimate a boundary from the distribution represented by the examples.

The proposed method learns a function that is positive inside the region and negative outside it. The function takes the form of a kernel expansion using a potentially small subset of training observations. Regularization controls the length of its weight vector in an associated feature space, connecting the desired simplicity of the region to a mathematical constraint on the function.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's statistical performance and present it as an extension of support vector learning to unlabelled data. The prescribed outside probability defines the estimation objective, rather than an automatically exact finite-sample outcome. The contribution is a support-vector formulation of novelty detection based on learning a region of typical observations.
neurips-1999-support-vector-method-for-n.tldr: A regularized kernel method learns a region of typical unlabelled observations with a specified target probability of falling outside.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why learning performance can improve in stages as the number of training examples increases. It uses a simple perceptron as a toy model and introduces structure into the distribution of its inputs. The aim is to isolate how properties of the data distribution can shape the learning curve.

The authors determine learning curves using statistical mechanics. They find stepwise generalization when the pattern distribution is highly anisotropic, meaning that its structure differs strongly across directions. In this setting, increasing the number of examples produces distinct stages in generalization behavior. The stated condition concerns pronounced directional differences in the inputs.

Although deliberately simple, the model appears to capture relevant features of a class of support vector machines previously observed to behave this way. This is a qualified connection between a tractable model and a more complex learning method. The contribution is an explanation of how structured input distributions can generate stepwise learning, rather than a claim that all support vector machines must generalize in stages.
neurips-1999-understanding-stepwise-gene.tldr: A perceptron toy model links highly anisotropic input distributions to stepwise generalization resembling behavior in a class of SVMs.

paragraphs: A hyperspectral image pixel can combine the reflectance spectra of several materials. The mixture coefficients represent how abundant those materials are within the pixel. This paper develops a probabilistic approach to recovering that mixture structure when the materials' reflectance characteristics are not known in advance, making the task unsupervised.

The model assumes that spectra combine linearly and that sensor noise is additive and normally distributed. Under these assumptions, the authors derive a maximum a posteriori framework. Prior information can encode requirements such as positive abundances and normalization, bringing constraints on material proportions directly into the estimation problem.

Different choices of prior information produce a family of algorithms rather than a single fixed procedure. In the noise-free case, one resulting algorithm can be interpreted as constrained independent component analysis. Simulations support the usefulness of the theory. The contribution is a common probabilistic formulation that connects unmixing assumptions, abundance constraints, and algorithm design, with the connection to constrained ICA stated specifically for the noise-free setting.
neurips-1999-unmixing-hyperspectral-data.tldr: A probabilistic framework uses linear-mixture assumptions and abundance priors to derive algorithms for unsupervised hyperspectral unmixing.
